## Quarto and GitHub Classroom

Most of the labs will be broken down into multiple tasks for you to complete.
We will extensively use **GitHub Classroom** to complete the labs.
We will talk about `git` and GitHub until Week 3, but for now you need to at least know how to get access to the lab files, so there are two commands you'll need to know.

Most of the code we write will be in `quarto`.
Quarto is a superset of `markdown`, that allows us to write documents made purely of plain text, and **compile** or **knit** them into formatted output, such as HTML or PDF.
Importantly, we can **embed `R` code** in `quarto` documents, have `quarto` run the code and embed the output of the code into the report.
This is important for reproducibility; the document we write contains all the documentation needed to explain the problem, the code to produce outputs and the interpretation of the outputs, in one place.

## Palmer Penguins in `R`

We will be using the Palmer Penguins dataset, a dataset that is an alternative to the classic Iris dataset.
It contains real observations of three penguin species - Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo - collected from the Palmer Station in Antarctica by researchers studying penguin ecology.
The dataset includes:

- Biological measurements (e.g. flipper length, body mass, bill depth)
- Metadata (species, island, sex, year)

This dataset was curated and made accessible by Allison Horst and collaborators, and has become popular in both R and Python data science communities.

The next code block loads and processes the dataset, stored in `penguins.csv` in the repository.

::: {.callout-tip}
If you look at the `.qmd` file in RStudio or VS Code, you will see the code appears surrounded by some backtick characters (\`).
These tell `quarto` that what is contained between the backticks is code.
The text after the backticks (`{r}`) tells us that this is `R` code.
When `quarto` compiles this document to HTML or PDF, the code is run, and the output is placed into the document.
:::

```{r}
#Load the library tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
#Read the penguins data and store it in penguins
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
#Show the first 6 rows of the data
head(penguins)
#Show the summary statistics for each column
summary(penguins)
#Plot body mass against flipper length, color by species
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
#Draw each penguin as a point (scatter plot)
  geom_point() +
#Use the minimal theme with a white background
  theme_minimal()
```

As flipper length increases, body mass tends to increase. Gentoo penguins have longer flippers and are heavier than the other two species. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap, so they are hard to tell apart using these two measurements.

### Tricks for Reproducibility

The code above is **not very well written**; it doesn't explain what is happening on each line. This is bad for reproducibility. Another scientist reading your code might not understand what is happening!

To improve this we can add *comments* to the code.
Comments are basically text that is ignored by the language, so that we can annotate it to explain it to other readers.

```{r}
# This is what a comment in R looks like
print("Hello world!")  # We can also add comments at the end of lines.
```

### Task 2 

- [ ] Add comments before each line of code in the blocks above, explaining what is happening on each line.
- [ ] Add some interpretation of the plot (in `markdown`, not as comments), after the code block.
- [ ] Create a second plot, below, that colours the dots by sex instead of by species.

```{r}
#Plot body mass against flipper length, colours by sex
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = sex)) +
#Draw each penguin as a point(scatter plot)
  geom_point() +
#Use the minimal theme with white background
  theme_minimal()
```

When flipper length increases, body mass tends to increase. Male penguins have longer flippers and are heavier than female penguins. Male and female penguins overlap when flipper length is between 170 and 220mm and body mass is between 3000 and 5000g. These grey points mean the missing values.

If you don't know how to do something in `R` you have a few options:

- Check the documentation, e.g. by using `?ggplot` or similar.
- Use a search engine to find an answer.
- Ask a Generative AI tool. Most of them are pretty good at coding.

The next task asks you to *extend* what we have already done using new functionality of `ggplot`.

- [ ] Create a third plot that uses colour for species and changes the *shape* of the points based on the sex.

```{r}
#Plot body mass against flipper length, colour by species, shape by sex
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species , shape = sex)) +
#Draw each penguin as a point(scatter plot)
  geom_point()
```

When flipper length increases, body mass tends to increase. The Gentoo penguins have longer flippers and have heavier body mass than Adelie penguins and Chinstrap. Within each species, male penguins (triangles point) are heavier than female penguins (circles points). 11 penguins with missing sex were removed from the plot.
